articles.headline: Start Your Next KMP App With Kotlin Toolchain 0.13
articles.dek: Kotlin Toolchain 0.13 introduces a unified CLI, recommended status, and built‑in cache components for faster KMP builds.

body.text: Key Takeaway

Kotlin Toolchain 0.13 ships a unified `kotlin‑toolchain` CLI that replaces the assorted Gradle wrappers and is now the recommended way to build KMP projects [FACT:9f119253f63b9f61b1622cbbfc2f514c][FACT:2466ce91f84b4a1895788b13d72a9eb7]. It adds a built‑in cache‑components suite that shares compiled artifacts across modules, which the team says will cut incremental build times for new codebases [FACT:45b6b2b19927cd09b958e84306491727][FACT:28bf44d73e1461cb0f681e3bd79dba26][FACT:0f6139163bd4c891c91a76c4423fb039]. The new `upgrade‑agent` command lets you bump the toolchain version across all sub‑projects with a single call [FACT:ab40e9bd05b0615943968038423da56b].
Why This Matters

Platform teams that spin up greenfield KMP services can now get a reproducible environment out of the box, avoiding the usual SDK‑version drift [FACT:0378a79dc23a550105b767ccff932f8b][FACT:78bdf7f603d76520aee01ed89e9fa827]. Because the toolchain is officially recommended, CI pipelines can standardize on the same binary, reducing cache‑misses and maintenance overhead [FACT:2466ce91f84b4a1895788b13d72a9eb7].
What Happened

Earlier this year the Kotlin team released an alpha version of the toolchain, but it was not generally recommended until this 0.13 GA [FACT:90d69d375eae9dd82eabf30d6f3deec2][FACT:7fce3f649abe6daf05eea1a9f31fe27e]. The 0.13 release bundles the cache components and upgrade‑agent, and the CLI now auto‑detects missing SDKs and installs them on supported hosts [FACT:78bdf7f603d76520aee01ed89e9fa827][FACT:0f6139163bd4c891c91a76c4423fb039][FACT:ab40e9bd05b0615943968038423da56b].
Builder View

If you’re wiring up a new KMP service, replace your old Gradle wrappers with `./kotlin-toolchain` and let the cache components handle artifact sharing across modules [FACT:9f119253f63b9f61b1622cbbfc2f514c][FACT:45b6b2b19927cd09b958e84306491727][FACT:28bf44d73e1461cb0f681e3bd79dba26]. Run `kotlin-toolchain upgrade-agent` when you want to align all sub‑projects – no manual version bumps needed [FACT:ab40e9bd05b0615943968038423da56b]. The CLI will auto‑detect missing SDKs and install them, meaning a fresh checkout builds out‑of‑the‑box on CI [FACT:78bdf7f603d76520aee01ed89e9fa827].
Ardur Take

Two independent sources confirm the unified entry point, the recommended status, and the cache‑components rollout, giving this update high confidence. Platform engineers should pilot the 0.13 toolchain on any new KMP codebase and consider a staged roll‑out for existing services to capture the build‑time savings [FACT:9f119253f63b9f61b1622cbbfc2f514c][FACT:2466ce91f84b4a1895788b13d72a9eb7][FACT:45b6b2b19927cd09b958e84306491727][FACT:28bf44d73e1461cb0f681e3bd79dba26][FACT:0f6139163bd4c891c91a76c4423fb039].

articles.headline: Argo CD v3.6.0‑rc2 lands with signed provenance and a trimmed quick‑start
articles.dek: The new release candidate bumps gitops‑engine, expands OCI chart support, and removes the manual namespace step.

body.text: Key Takeaway

Argo CD v3.6.0‑rc2 appears on GitHub, bumping gitops‑engine to the same version and tightening image provenance so you can verify which CLI binaries built each container [FACT:bc86c40bc0086293f580f0378a169335][FACT:4c60791910e73c8815ba7fbf0570b268].
Why This Matters

When you need an audit trail for CI‑generated images, the new provenance payload records the exact build tools, cutting the time spent chasing unsigned artifacts [FACT:4c60791910e73c8815ba7fbf0570b268].
What Happened

The accompanying release‑notes blog post lists three concrete changes: a quick‑start that no longer requires a manual ‘kubectl create namespace’ step [FACT:9acaca76679f6ff08113ca53c16e65f5], support for both HTTP and HTTPS OCI chart repositories [FACT:56e45729933213401b2c43552f2b1b63], and a Helm‑plugin that is now registered under its own directory for easier path handling [FACT:d30fe5677d9a48fab2f734b50bcd4dff] [FACT:e21a7639e04cb7c5e80d7acb74121661].
Builder View

If your onboarding scripts still run ‘kubectl create namespace’, you can drop that line and let the built‑in quick‑start set up the namespace for you [FACT:9acaca76679f6ff08113ca53c16e65f5]. OCI‑based Helm charts can now be fetched over plain HTTP as well as HTTPS, so you don’t need a TLS‑terminating proxy for internal registries [FACT:56e45729933213401b2c43552f2b1b63]. Build pipelines that invoke the Helm plugin will find the binary in a predictable plugins/ folder, removing the need for custom symlinks [FACT:d30fe5677d9a48fab2f734b50bcd4dff].
Open Questions

The UI filter currently returns a generic ‘Sorry, something went wrong’ message on a few dashboards; the team has flagged it for the next patch [FACT:46afc9741e8f55893ba45c0d5cfdf067]. It remains to be seen whether the richer provenance data adds noticeable overhead to large‑scale image builds [FACT:4c60791910e73c8815ba7fbf0570b268].
Ardur Take

One verified source confirms the RC contents, and the changes are low‑risk, so spin up a staging cluster, apply the new manifests, and verify the GPG signature [FACT:bc86c40bc0086293f580f0378a169335][FACT:43944bc428ffbb69ca60a7535b2b3733].

articles.headline: Harbor v2.14.5 tightens image signing and webhook policy – what builders need to know
articles.dek: v2.14.5 makes Cosign signatures mandatory, adds a webhook address opt‑out, and ships extra Helm env‑vars.

body.text: Key Takeaway

Harbor 2.14.5 forces projects to accept only Cosign‑signed images and makes the previously‑broken internal‑address webhook check optional – you’ll see push failures or webhook warnings unless you sign your images or flip the new opt‑out flag [FACT:381959f9ff9839cfd3d72358d6d13d75][FACT:919abb2a44f075f751b0e68ce174b268][FACT:fa3da90406f1043e6967c6313172604b][FACT:8ac6c16e1fe3115518e0ab019eb9e842].
Why This Matters

Mandatory signing stops vulnerable binaries from slipping into CI pipelines, and the webhook change prevents accidental denial‑of‑service when internal URLs are used – both directly protect production workloads [FACT:ca5d8626446742dde033571d665c7e4e][FACT:fa3da90406f1043e6967c6313172604b].
What Happened

The release notes spell out three concrete changes: (1) any push of an unsigned image now fails with a ‘Precondition Failed’ response [FACT:919abb2a44f075f751b0e68ce174b268]; (2) internal‑address webhook validation is guarded by a new opt‑out flag that you can enable via Helm values [FACT:fa3da90406f1043e6967c6313172604b][FACT:8ac6c16e1fe3115518e0ab019eb9e842]; (3) Helm charts now expose extra environment variables for Harbor‑YAML integrations, letting you tweak core settings without editing the chart directly [FACT:971d9f52f5b5821805b4b46150fda6c5].
Builder View

If your pipelines still push plain Docker images, add a Cosign signing step or temporarily enable the project‑wide ‘allow unsigned’ toggle – the toggle is still honored but will be phased out [FACT:75cd9374a37cd19f2e92b857de4a8978]. Update your Helm release with `--set webhook.internalAddressOptOut=true` to keep existing webhook URLs alive [FACT:8ac6c16e1fe3115518e0ab019eb9e842]. The new env vars (`HARBOR_CORE_*`) let you inject custom Harbor settings without a chart rewrite [FACT:971d9f52f5b5821805b4b46150fda6c5].
Open Questions

Will the opt‑out flag be retired in the next minor version? How will Harbor quarantine existing unsigned images after the rollout? The notes don’t cover performance impact of the extra signature verification step [FACT:381959f9ff9839cfd3d72358d6d13d75].
